title: Brandi Carlile’s All-Requests Tour Isn’t Just a Magnificent Stunt, but an Unusually Moving Transaction Between Performer and Audience: Concert Review
description: Is it possible to plan for magic, serendipity, peak-level proficiency and finally sublimity by… really not planning at all? That is the question.
body:
Is it possible to plan for magic, serendipity, peak-level proficiency and finally sublimity by… really not planning at all? That is the question. On Brandi Carlile‘s current “Burn the Setlist!” tour, the answer is clear: Sometimes Shangri-La really is best reached with a lost roadmap.

	The shortish 19-date outing Carlile is undertaking at the moment is the first all-requests tour in memory by any artist significant enough to have it show up on our radar. It might even be a historic first, as far as a proven headliner opting to play nothing but spontaneously generated live audience picks. Which is odd when you think about it, because doesn’t anyone who’s been to a lot of shows over the years have a favorite moment when a star got loose and succumbed to someone shouting out a favorite (though they usually don’t want to encourage that kind of behavior?). But at the opposite end of the scale from bar bands and tip jars, doing solely requests sounds like as much of a nightmare to most performers as it does a dream to hardcore fans. There are perfectly good reasons not to throw the song selections completely open to stans for roughly 2 hours and 40 minutes — as Carlile and her two bandmates, Phil and Tim Hanseroth, are doing now — when you have a recorded catalog of close to a hundred original songs, plus a repertoire of proven live cover choices.

	Who among even the greats of music has anything close to 100% recall? When the recent and distant pasts are both being dredged up, a good corollary to “Never let ’em see you sweat” might be: Never let ’em see you forget.

	Fortunately, Brandi Carlile and the Hanseroth twins are freaking elephants.



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	But making a point out of not planning is different from not being prepared. And Carlile and the brothers are prepared for this, first of all, by having brain chemistry that is clearly a little bit different from mine or probably yours, with the power not just to generate constant creative sparks but to put those sparks in an easily accessible lockbox. You’re either genetically predisposed to that kind of recall or you’re not, and at least a little part of why Carlile and the Hanseroths have been ideal partners since the turn of the millennium is that shared gift. Not that they came into the “Burn the Setlist!” tour relying completely on muscle memory. Tim Hanseroth posted an IG video of himself running through their studio albums and strumming along to stir the old juices. Carlile said in a video livestream for fans on the tour’s eve that she would have a monitor for lyrics if she needed it. But at the show I caught, I barely noticed Carlile looking down at it… which I can’t say for most big tours I attend where the show is locked in for months straight.

	All of this risks making the tour seem like a stunt, which it kind of is. But the bigger reason for why it’s such a rousing success — and a reason why fans may remember these shows almost as well as Carlile and company remember their songs — is how many deeply moving moments are stirred up up in the shows, in the quietest bits that come between the outbreaks of hysterical shouting and sign-waving. Leaving the setlists up to fans, chance or God results in obscure picks and ironic juxtapositions that sometimes aren’t anything more than fun or curious, but are sometimes unexpectedly touching in a way that one of Carlile’s perfectly laid-out arena shows probably couldn’t be. Not just a mere test of skills, these concerts are really a nightly emotional chemistry experiment. On the right night — and the show I saw in Oakland was the right night — it might be transcendent, in a way that’s a little different even from the transcendent gigs we’ve seen before.


	Carlile had some notes before the show began; rather than restrictions, felt like promissory instructions about how to best proceed through a candy store about to open. “I can see your signs all the way back, and I will call on people all the way in the back,” Carlile declared at the top of the concert Nov. 7 at the Fox Oakland, the second on their tour. (She later made good on that, picking more people from the rear balcony than any other part of the audience, though the front rows did OK too.).”Everything is pretty much fair game,” she instructed — “any song that we’ve ever done.” She noted that they wouldn’t be open to attempting songs they’d never performed even once before, “so we’re not gonna be able to ‘Free Bird’ or ‘Sweet Home Alabama’ this shit. But we might be able to get away with the handful of covers we’ve done in the past. And listen,” she added reassuringly, “you don’t have to worry about me — I’m 45, so if there’s a song I don’t want to do, I will just say no.”

	But Carlile also wanted it understood that this was not meant to be a tricky pop quiz. “Don’t feel like this should be a ‘stump the band’-type deal,” she said. “We really want this to be musically awesome for you guys. We want you to love what you’re hearing and request the songs that you really want to hear. I’m a deep cuts girl. I love track 7 on everyone’s album. I’m a last track gal. And I know that you know that you’re never gonna hear those songs on the big tours that we do.” That said, she opened it up to the idea that predictability isn’t always a negative. “If you want to hear the fucking ‘Story,'” Carlile declared, “just request ‘The Story’!”


	No one chosen in Oakland wanted to choose the fucking “Story,” or “The Joke” or anything else that might qualify as too big a hit, possibly in fear of eliciting groans from a rarities-inclined audience. (It does feel safe to call her biggest songs hits, even if toward the end, listening to the roars for obscurities, she said, “It almost makes up for the fact that we never had a hit. If you’ve never had a hit, all your songs get to be hits with your buddies. I don’t think we need one.”) But Carlile stating her openness to doing more predictable songs did create a safety net for the audience, establishing that there would be no wrong answers or incorrect pleas.
	

	Also no duds, although one song choice did pose an unsolved mystery, with its unexpected popularity, which was resolved with a bit of discussion between performers and audience. A couple in the front row of the Fox Oakland’s balcony requested “Heart’s Content,” which got only light applayse Carlile then noted had also been requested the previous night in Portland… to her puzzlement. “I think this song’s gonna be requested every night,” she laughed, “because we never play it and it’s to me the most obscure song. Is it even on one of our albums?” It is — from 14 years ago — but it’s understandable why it’s never been a concert favorite: Perfectly pleasant-sounding, it’s the rare tune in her 21-year catalog that just doesn’t really sound like a Brandi Carlile. Phil Hanseroth relayed reportage from someone in the front rows: “It’s in a movie.” “What’s the movie?” “Safe Haven.” “Is it a romcom?” inquired Carlile. “Is it sad, like ‘The Notebook?’ Well, thank you — now I understand… A bunch of romcom fans up in here.” No judgments.
	

	There was a greater sense of consensus, on-stage and off-, about most of the rest of the 22 songs played in Oakland. The first chosen was “Raising Hell,” a rowdy oldie that made it clear that, among other things, Carlile and the twins have always harbored stomp-and-holler tendencies… with literal stomping, on a few occasions in this set, to add percussion into the mix. In the most extreme pendulum swing possible, next up among the requests was a song about raising heaven, “The Mother,” a gorgeously happy song that deals with motherhood very generally and gay motherhood very specifically.

	Carlile preceded “The Mother” with an extended anecdote about chaperoning the social life of her eldest daughter, who’s repeatedly named in the chorus — with a side note that the story should not leave the room, since Evangeline is at the age where it’s not easy to always discern whether she resents being talked about on stage or takes pride in it in any given moment. That alone, in the singer’s mind, justified the decision to have phones put away in Yondr pouches, something Carlile has not required at any of her previous gigs but wanted for these, both to create greater intimacy and to keep flubs from going up on YouTube. (There weren’t any blatant ones, although the Hanseroths did shoot knowing smiles at each other a couple of times when a note sounded a little bit interesting.)

	Carlile has often spoken before “The Mother” in concert, but the loose formatting of this show seemed to allow her to stretch out even more, over a period of minutes. “I remember having a really difficult time with it because Catherine carried both girls… Somebody talked me through it and told me I needed to come up with a mantra. And my mantra became, I have to tell myself I’m a mother so that I can believe I deserve to call myself that. So it became ‘I am the mother of Evangeline.’ And when I first wrote this song, I thought, ‘Well, this thing’s niche! You have to be a gay mom that didn’t carry a child to understand this song.’ And it’s not true — it’s a universal thing — because here I am in Oakland, and this man stood up and wanted me to play the song.”

	The mood swings got wilder from there, as “Folsom Prison Blues” was requested next, a cover Carlile figured they hadn’t done in a decade. (Actually, only seven years.) The twins spent a bit of time remember and working out the licks before a formal kickoff that led to some wildly exuberant death in Reno. From there, in another big turnabout, it was “Dying Day,” which they opted to do at the lip of the stage, without amplification, as they’d done in the distant past, albeit probably in slightly smaller rooms than the 2,800-capacity Fox. Voices carried.
	

	The tour offers an opportunity to witness problem-solving in real time. For Carlile and the twins, perhaps the biggest problem was obliging a request for Alanis Morissette’s “Uninvited.” This was not because of recent unfamiliarity with the tune — they performed it nearly every night on this year’s “Human” arena tour, among the encores — but because they’d never done it as an acoustic trio. Without the heightened drama of a string section and the number’s signature piano notes. “I have no idea how we’re gonna do this without strings. Love will find a way,” Carlile said. “And no piano? That’s the whole song!” But she and the brothers found their path to make it a pure guitar-and-bass rock ‘n’ roll scorcher, followed by an exultant “We don’t need no stinking strings!” (With implicit apologies, undoubtedly, to SistaStrings.)



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
	



	“I Belong With You” was introduced as having been written “when I first met my wife, Catherine… I wasn’t a big love song girl. I didn’t really get them.” The monologue was interrupted when she went to greet a young girl in the front row who was having her own emotional moment. Hi babe. What’s goin’ on?… Don’t cry!” When she came back, she dropped the love-story intro, but did have some instructions for the Hanseroths: “You guys aren’t on in this one until four minutes.” They took five for four, and you didn’t have to look at your watch — but just for fun, I did — to know that she was right on target with her reminder to the bros, give or take 10 seconds. This was a woman who knows her own material, as was repeatedly evident when each request was immediately followed by a callout to her guitar tech about which instrument to bring out. (“That’s gonna be capo 8 for a strummer”… “‘That Year’ is gonna be Kalamazoo, capo 7.”)

	Carlile sang “Turpentine,” a song about physically battling with her brother growing up, with its wistful rejoinder, “I’m warning you, we’re growing up” — and though she didn’t directly make the connection this night, it was easy to surmise how growing up to close to her “Irish twin” brother prepared her for a life and career with the Hanseroth twins. She taled about writing “Stranger at My Door” in Australia, “jetlagged with a broken heart,” and bringing the new song to the twins in a club’s backstage alley. “‘Tell me the truth. Is it too much? Is it too many words?’ Phil’s like, ‘Eh, it’s a little wordy.’ Phil’s a 7 on the Enneogram. You know what that means?… You’re incredibly impatient, and this song is five minutes long and full of words and that’s why you guys love it!” she laughed, turning to the attending Bramily.
	

	Dolly Parton was saluted with “Jolene” — “She had a temper, she had a dirty mouth, and she had the biggest heart in the world,” said Carlile — and a call-out for some Joni Mitchell on that singer’s birthday went rewarded with an E-major “River.” The singer talked about a two-and-a-half-hour phone call while driving home on Halloween night, hearing even more wild stories from the legend than she’d already heard. “A lot of times she’ll end the story by going, ‘And that was where I found “Refuge of the Roads.”‘ Or, ‘And that’s why I shouldn’t have got on that plane.’ In those moments, I realized that, no matter what happens in my life, I got to listen to Joni Mitchell play solitaire and tell me her stories. She’s not lying. I’m not even sure she’s capable of it.”

	The last stretch of the Oakland concert lifted the show from delightful travelogue to a something heavier on some of the trio’s most emotionally incisive songs, although it was difficult to know whether they were making these selections intentionally or those requests were providentially just arriving right on time. Tim Hanseroth did say he’d been waiting all night to pick on the guy in the front rows holding a sign asking for “The Things I Regret,” and subsequently showed up on Instagram thanking the fan again. It raised one of those questions that can only arise at a rarities-filled show like this: Why was this not a bigger hit — even amongst the band itself? It’s got an unforgettable singalong hook and serious stomp-and-holler bona fides, and it’s about the accumulation of screw-ups that adds up to a lifetime’s worth. What more could you ask?



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	But the most touching highlights were “Most of All,” a song about seeing your family in yourself (there are few lines more evocative than “His heavy hands swing at the end of my arms”)… and “That Year,” an alternately chilling and warm ballad about looking to make peace with a high school friend who committed suicide, from across the veil that separates the living and the dead. And the recent “No One Knows Us,” about how each friendship bond formed among young people is precious, irreplaceable and worth the upkeep in a more depressed middle age. And the penultimate number, “That Wasn’t Me,” a neo-gospel ballad so healing and cathartic, it would have become Carlile’s signature song in some other lifetime, instead of a deep cut.

	The actual climax? A rare cover of Led Zeppelin’s “Going to California,” because Carlile can hit the golden-god notes. And then California surrendered the combo to the next stop in Tucson. (Where they did not get the Led out, of course, and where the next stop involved only repeating four of the 22 numbers heard in Oakland.)
	

	As a cherry on top, anyone leaving the show each night finds that there was a bonus offered earlier, not to them, but to anyone suffering at home with FOMO. Right before she takes the stage, when the local audience is already seated, Carlile does a livestream of a single song while she’s having her makeup applied, just for everyone who doesn’t have the privilege of the live show (though, of course, the concert crowd can catch up with it later). It’s a hell of a miniature grace note.

	Saying this was the best show I’ve ever seen by Carlile and company probably without saying, after saying all of that; at times, I got to thinking it was one of the best shows I’ve ever seen from anyone, out of untold thousands. Concert hyperbole is a dangerous thing, but I found myself hard-pressed to recall comparable instances in which I’d seen rock ‘n’ roll performers so throughly committed to the moment, not just for a moment but for close to three hours of them. Maybe that’s because I have a worse memory than Carlile and the Hanseroths, but more likely because this really is as good as it gets, if you have a taste for the rare intersection where hair-trigger meets tear-jerk. Adjust your settings for how many hundreds of dollars you’d pay for a resale ticket for the remaining dates accordingly.



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	Setlist for Brandi Carlile at the Fox Oakland, November 2026:
	

	Raise HellThe MotherFolsom Prison Blues (Johnny Cash cover)Dying DayHeart’s ContentUninvited (Alanis Morissette cover)I Belong to YouHumanTurpentineHard Way HomeI WillThe Stranger at My DoorMost of AllJolene (Dolly Parton cover)That YearRiver (Joni Mitchell cover)The Things I RegretCloser to You/I’ve Just Seen a Face (Beatles cover)No One Knows UsBeginning to Feel the YearsThat Wasn’t MeGoing to California (Led Zeppelin)

title: Oak Ridge Boys’ Richard Sterban, Whose Distinctive Bass Voice Powered ‘Elvira’ and Other Country Smashes, Dies at 83
description: Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Oak Ridge Boys, died Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn., following complications from bronchitis and pneum
body:
Richard Sterban, the bass vocalist of the Oak Ridge Boys, died Saturday in Hendersonville, Tenn., following complications from bronchitis and pneumonia after a battle with cancer. He was 83.

	Both his family and the band announced his death. “We appreciate all of your love, support, and prayers. Please continue to lift us up in this difficult time, we find comfort knowing that he is currently face to face with Jesus,” wrote his family.
	

	Sterban joined the Oak Ridge Boys as the group’s bass singer in 1972 after previous member Noel Fox left the band. Alongside lead singer Duane Allen, baritone William Lee Golden and tenor Joe Bonsall, Sterban helped complete the gospel quartet. The group placed 34 singles in the country Top 10, 17 of them at No. 1, earned Grammy, Country Music Association and Academy of Country Music awards, and became members of the Grand Ole Opry, the Gospel Music Hall of Fame and the Country Music Hall of Fame. Sterban’s voice was the foundation of the group’s four-part harmonies, particularly apparent on the famous song “Elvira,” among others.

	Before he joined the Oak Ridge Boys, he helped found the Keystones, a gospel quartet, before joining J.D. Sumner and the Stamps Quartet, which Elvis Presley hired to sing behind him for about a year and a half.

	Sterban was born April 24, 1943, in Camden, New Jersey. He began singing at age six in Sunday school and sang tenor in his seventh-grade glee club. After graduating from Collingswood High School, he studied music at Trenton State College.

	Sterban is survived by his wife, Donna; his daughters, Lauren (Tyler) and Tori (Michael); his sons, Rich (Chele), Doug, and Chris; his grandchildren, Mali (Zachary), Nikolas, Tyler (Ryann), Madelyn, Alexandra, Rex, Owen, and Charli Grace; and his great-grandchildren, Salem, Asher, and Theo. He was preceded in death by his mother, Victoria, brother, Joseph, and grandson, Zachary.
	

	Funeral arrangements will be announced at a later date.

title: Dawn Greenhalgh, Canadian Stage Veteran Who Voiced the Queen in ‘Babar,’ Dies at 93
description:
Dawn Greenhalgh, a veteran Canadian actress of stage, film and television, died Nov. 6 in Toronto. She was 93.

	Born in Shanghai, China, she spent
body:
Dawn Greenhalgh, a veteran Canadian actress of stage, film and television, died Nov. 6 in Toronto. She was 93.

	Born in Shanghai, China, she spent her childhood with her family in a Japanese prisoner of war camp, where she discovered a love for music, theater and dance. Greenhalgh moved to Canada with only a guardian at the age of 14, attending Montreal High School and beginning her performing career.


	In 1953, at 19 years old, she became a founding member of Canada’s Stratford Festival. She went on to become a founding member of the Neptune Theatre in Halifax and Theatre Plus in Toronto. She performed on stages around the world and in New York studied with Uta Haagen, Herbert Berghof and Mira Rostova. 
	

	Greenhalgh’s film roles included Sofia Coppola‘s “The Virgin Suicides” and David Cronenberg’s “Map to the Stars.” She also worked with her daughter, Megan Follows, in the popular Canadian series “Anne of Green Gables.” Other television appearances included “Five Days at Memorial,” “Saving Hope” and “La Femme Nikita.” She voiced Queen Celeste, Babar the elephant’s wife, on the animated series “Babar.”

	With the Stratford Festival, she performed in plays including “All’s Well That Ends Well” with Alec Guinness, “Antony and Cleopatra” and “Love’s Labour’s Lost.”

	“Dawn Greenhalgh was a powerhouse, a dynamic, brilliant actress,” Stratford Festival Artistic Director Antoni Cimolino wrote on Instagram. “As an extraordinary artist she could be both charming and unsettling. It was a pleasure to hear her perspective on plays and productions as it was informed by a lifetime of wide experience, a sparkling intellect and an independent, free thinking mind.”
	

	She is survived by her children Edwina Follows; Laurence Follows; Samantha Follows and Megan Follows, six grandchildren and two step-grandchildren.

schema.headline: Dawn Greenhalgh, Canadian Stage Veteran Who Voiced the Queen in ‘Babar,’ Dies at 93

title: Philippines Wins Inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Thailand
description:
The Philippines has won the first ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

	Carmelle, representing the Phillippines, scooped first place with the track
body:
The Philippines has won the first ever Eurovision Song Contest Asia.

	Carmelle, representing the Phillippines, scooped first place with the track “Sobra-Sobra,” earning 211 points.

	She beat Thailand’s act Mang x Daou, who came second place with 179 points, and Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên, who took third place with 164 points. Malaysia and Laos rounded out the top five.


	The first ever Asian edition of the contest was held Saturday in the Thai capital of Bangkok. Eleven countries took part, including Cambodia, Mongolia and Korea. Like the European edition, which recently celebrated 70 years, points were awarded via a combination of national juries and public vote.
	

	A “rest of the world” vote also awarded a set of points equivalent to that of one participating country, with audiences from 183 countries and territories worldwide having their say.

	The contest was aired in the participating countries as well as on Eurovision’s official YouTube channel. EBU members TVP (Poland), Sveriges Radio (Sweden), Kan (Israel) and SBS (Australia) also broadcast the contest, which was hosted by Thai TV stars Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop.

	As well as the competing countries, Thai superstar Jeff Satur performed alongside this year’s Eurovision winner Dara, who took first place for Bulgaria in the May contest with her track “Bangaranga.” The show, which also included a special opening performance celebrating the host city, was produced by Voxovation and Bangkok-based S20 Productions. It was sponsored by Zoop.

	“Congratulations to Carmelle and the Philippines on becoming the first-ever winners of Eurovision Song Contest Asia,” said Eurovision director Martin Green. “What an historic achievement! This inaugural edition was a major milestone and brought together an extraordinary range of musical talent, cultures and creative voices from across the region.” 
	

	“As we celebrate 70 years of the Eurovision Song Contest, seeing its spirit of unity through music take on a new life in Asia is a significant moment, and one we hope will inspire artists and audiences for years to come.”

	Assaf Blecher, exec producer of Eurovision Song Contest Asia, said: “Bringing the first Eurovision Song Contest Asia to life in Bangkok has been an extraordinary journey.”

	“Congratulations to Carmelle and the Philippines on making history as our first-ever winners. This is just the beginning of an exciting new chapter for Eurovision in Asia.”

schema.headline: Philippines Wins Inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Thailand

title: Hoobastank, Simple Plan and More Bands Performed Mid-Flight During Nationwide Air Travel Ground Stop
description: Southwest Airlines brought back its “Live at 35” program during Friday’s nationwide grounding of air travel with performances from artists on their
body:
Southwest Airlines brought back its “Live at 35” program during Friday’s nationwide grounding of air travel with performances from artists on their way to Vans Warped Tour.

	Hoobastank, The Used, Simple Plan and Lolo performed aboard a Southwest flight from Los Angeles to Orlando, Fla., on Nov. 13 as part of the music program, which hosts surprise midflight pop-up performances. The flight left Los Angeles around 11 a.m., about two hours before the FAA declared a national ground stop that snarled global travel and left more than 1 million people stranded.
	

	Hoobastank took to the aisles at cruising altitude for a live rendition of their 2004 hit “The Reason.” Passengers sang along and posted about the performance on social media. Lolo, who played at Warped Tour’s Long Beach, Calif., stop in July, wrote “Every plane was grounded today, but the emo gods made sure this one flew.”

	The sky-high performance came amid a nationwide ground stop for all flights, with the Federal Aviation Administration citing “extraordinary circumstances.” The initial alert came just after 1 p.m. PT on Friday, stranding some 1.5 million travelers by CNN’s estimate. Airborne flights were allowed to continue, but new domestic flights were delayed or canceled, throwing travel plans into question for various industry events over the weekend. The stop was lifted about five hours later, shortly before 6 p.m. PT.

	The “Live at 35” artists were in route to the final Vans Warped Tour 2026 stop in Orlando, which runs Nov. 14-15 at Camping World Stadium Campus. The Warped Tour expanded from three to five locations in 2026, with two-day festivals in Washington, D.C., Long Beach and Orlando, Fla. alongside two new international sites in Montreal and Mexico City.
	

	Founded in 1995, Vans Warped Tour has become a definitive rock and alt festival, featuring 100+ artists across rock, pop punk, alternative, emo and more genres. Past performers include Blink-182, No Doubt, Sublime, Beck, Katy Perry, NOFX, Limp Bizkit, Black Eyed Peas, Green Day, Eminem, Yellowcard, Bad Religion and more.

	(Pictured: Doug Robb and Dan Estrin of Hoobastank)

title: Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced His Second Mid-Show Departure
description: Journey drummer Deen Castronovo is out of the band, the group announced Friday, due to health issues that caused him to have to drop out of two sh
body:
Journey drummer Deen Castronovo is out of the band, the group announced Friday, due to health issues that caused him to have to drop out of two shows mid-concert in the space of just over a month, the latest of which was Tuesday night in Boston. 

	After he was replaced by his drum tech as an emergency fill-in partway through the Tuesday Boston show, the band performed Thursday night in Cleveland with a new drummer, Steve Murphy. On Friday, the group finally addressed the issue in a statement and said that Murphy would be stepping into Castronovo’s shoes as their full-time drummer going forward.

	The band’s social media post read: “Dear Friends… After careful consideration and an extensive year of touring, our talented, longtime drummer Deen Castronovo has decided to step away to focus on personal health matters that require his attention. He has our full support during this time and extends his heartfelt thanks to the fans for the love, encouragement, and kindness he has received. Native New Yorker Steve Murphy, who comes to us from working with bands such as Alan Parsons Project, Trans Siberian Orchestra, Christopher Cross and Jack Bruce, will be joining us for the remainder of November. We look forward to continuing to share unforgettable nights of music with all of you.”

	The post did not include any photos of Castronovo, but did include shots of Murphy celebrating his first show with the band Thursday.

	The message was also shared on Castronovo’s personal Facebook page. The drummer did not offer any additional comment of his own beyond the band’s statement, but none might have been expected, as he has previously noted he leaves it to someone else to oversee his social media accounts.

	Castronovo, 62, who joined Journey in 1998, had to leave Tuesday’s show in Boston 12 songs into the show, according to reports posted on Setlists.fm. He was replaced for the rest of the truncated set by a fill-in, his drum tech, Steve Toomey, just as he had been a month earlier under similar circumstances in Tulsa. The length of Tuesday’s show was cut down from the usual 29 or so songs to 20, with eight songs following Castronovo’s stage departure. 


	On Oct. 8 in Oklahoma, he left the stage after just two songs and was hospitalized; Toomey also completed the show that night. Whatever was ailing Castronovo was not explained to the public. But at that time the band said publicly that he quickly bounced back and was in fighting trim to resume the tour. Castronovo indeed played their next show on Oct. 10 without incident, as he did all the subsequent shows through Nov. 7, before apparently falling ill again mid-show Tuesday.

	Castronovo joined Journey in 1998 to replace original drummer Steve Smith. He was forced out of the group in 2015 after being charged with assaulting a woman, and was replaced at that time by Omar Hakim. He subsequently had nine charges dismissed and pleaded guilty to six others, receiving a suspended sentence. He came back to rejoin the Journey lineup in 2021, after performing with guitarist Neal Schon on a side-project tour in 2019.


	In 2023, the drummer explained his perseonal journey in and out of Journey — and back in — in an interview with Ultimate Classic Rock. “I had to take some time off and, pardon my language, get my shit together. I was a mess, and it was horrible what happened. But today, I’m doing great, clean and sober, working hard, doing what I need to do – and I put God first, family second. My job is third, where before it was all the other way around: ‘I want to be a rocker, I want to play music and I want to party,’ and everything was on the back burner – everything else, which is really sad. … I was so wrapped up in drugs and alcohol; family was way down the line. That was heartbreaking. But here I am today, and family is most important, and my job is great. I love what I do with Journey and I love what I do with Revolution Saints, but the beautiful thing is what I learned the most, being in treatment, is that if it all went away, you know what? I’m still all right. … I love playing, but if it was all to go away tomorrow, God bless, man. Life goes on, and I’m OK with myself. I’m comfortable in my skin.”
	

	There are eight shows left on Journey’s 2026 tour, including a Saturday night stop in Greenville, before the band wraps up the touring year Nov. 28 in San Francisco. Journey had previously announced this as part of a farewell tour, but Schon said recently that the long goodbye was going so well, they had plans to proceed indefinitely.

	“Your love, energy and passion for this music have reminded us how much we still share and how much this journey means to all of us,” Schon wrote. “What began as ‘The Final Frontier’ now feels more like ‘The Long Goodbye.’ We’re letting our hearts — and the connection we feel with you every night — help guide what comes next.”

schema.headline: Journey Announces Drummer Deen Castronovo Is Exiting Band, Days After Another Health Scare Forced His Second Mid-Show Departure

title: Chris Pratt Says He ‘Would Love’ James Gunn to Direct a Fourth ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ Film After DC Exit
description: Chris Pratt thinks it would be “awesome” to reunite with James Gunn for a fourth “Guardians of the Galaxy” film after the director announced his de
body:
Chris Pratt thinks it would be “awesome” to reunite with James Gunn for a fourth “Guardians of the Galaxy” film after the director announced his departure from DC Studios this week.

	Gunn and his co-chief, Peter Safran, were ousted from their positions on Nov. 9 following David Ellison’s Skydance merger in October. Marvel Studios alum Jeremy Latcham was announced as the new president and chief creative officer of DC Studios.
	

	The executive shuffle marks another setback for DC Studios, which has struggled to compete with the powerhouse that is Disney’s Marvel Cinematic Universe of late. But it opens a route for Gunn to return to the MCU, where he directed three “Guardians of the Galaxy” movies.

	Pratt recently told Moviezine that he would love to reunite with Gunn for a fourth film in the franchise. “That would be awesome. I love working with James. He’s the man,” Pratt said when asked about the possibility of making the film. “I haven’t had a chance to speak with him since that news came out yesterday…. It’s always tough because anytime something like this comes up, it could always become a headline.”

	He continued: “All I’ll say is I love James. He directed all three movies, and that’s pretty rare… so if he wanted to come back and bring it back, I would love that.”

	Pratt has starred as Star-Lord in the franchise across six films, with 2014’s “Guardians of the Galaxy,” “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2,” “Avengers: Infinity War,” “Avengers: Endgame,” “Thor: Love and Thunder” and most recently in “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3.”
	

	The Guardians of the Galaxy last graced the screens of viewers in 2023’s “Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3,” which promised via end-credits text that Star-Lord would return. Pratt has been vocal about his pitches to bring the character back and confirmed in October that the studio has taken “hard action” to make it happen.

schema.headline: Chris Pratt Says He ‘Would Love’ James Gunn to Direct a Fourth ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ Film After DC Exit

title: Inside the First AI Music Awards, a Chaotic Evening Attempting to Normalize Tech-Assisted Tunes
description: I knew things were a little off when the first thing I heard on my walk to the AI Music Awards was “the winner…” followed by the sweet voice of Kel
body:
I knew things were a little off when the first thing I heard on my walk to the AI Music Awards was “the winner…” followed by the sweet voice of Kelly Clarkson.

	No, Miss American Idol did not abandon her feud with the Brooklyn bird to capitalize on her newfound appreciation for AI. But as I approached the Mayan Theater in Downtown Los Angeles on a sunny afternoon to check in for Friday’s inaugural “AI Music Awards,” powered by the “Sonic Intelligence Academy” or “SIQA,” I wondered if her voice was so strong as to echo through the nearly century-old theater-turned-nightclub’s walls. Alas, not so: It was Clarkson’s Christmas classic “Underneath the Tree,” playing from speakers at a local YWCA event across the street.
	

	To qualify for the awards, artists needed to register their tracks to SIQA’s “Verified Registry,” which denotes whether the song was fully AI-generated, made with the assistance of AI or featured a cloned human voice to lead the tune (what the group calls a “human + AI hybrid”).

	Registered artists then nominate their peers in the 25 categories up for consideration — everything from “AI Song of the Year” to “Best AI Pop Song” to “Best AI Comedic Song” — and then vote on the winners. One of those nominees was Xania Monet, the AI persona of Telisha “Nikki” Jones, who a day earlier won the AI Album of the Year category at SIQA’s inaugural summit and who would eventually go on to win both artist and song of the year, three out of four of the awards’ top categories. (The fourth, producer of the year, went to “DJ Shawn Q.”)
	

	The Sonic Intelligence Academy is the brainchild of software engineer Timirah “TJ” James and her sister Mia James. Since its January launch, it has worked to establish an awards program to counter the mainstream music industry’s aversion to AI. The group believes there needs to be infrastructure that supports those using AI to create music, rather than dismissing its existence, and it hopes to be an AI counterpart to the longstanding Recording Academy that governs the Grammy Awards. It advocates for artists to publicly associate themselves with their AI-powered work, eager to highlight the humans who helped create the product.

	It’s a noble, if surprising, decision to embrace its role as counterculture when AI artists continue to pursue a Billboard charting position. Some of its methods are a little overt, perhaps intentionally: After some in the industry spurned the idea of AI-generated music charting on Billboard’s industry-standard charts, the group used a week in January ahead of the Grammys to launch its own charts exclusively for AI music. The Mayan is a 12-minute walk from the Crypto.com Arena, the Grammys’ longtime home.

	The moves are not subtle, but subtlety is not the organization’s goal. The group and awards’ existence alone reflects those in the AI music space trying to move past the thorny legal questions surrounding AI music, which have led to lawsuits by artists and record labels against generators like Suno and Udio over copyright infringement, and into a realm of relevance within the genres they’re trying to embody.

	It is, in a word, new, and new things mean kinks to work out.

	The first kink I noticed was when, as I arrived 30 minutes before the red carpet was set to begin, the doors to the venue were locked. I had to pull on each door before someone opened one, which led me to the check-in stand (bypassing any form of security, which didn’t seem to exist). I entered the foyer and arrived at the makeshift red carpet, where about 12, mostly independent media ventures set up cameras to interview the various nominees, presenters, and VIPs who’d grace the roughly 7-foot-long red carpet in front of one of the two step-and-repeat backdrops. A spokesperson told me 29 media outlets had signed up to cover the event, but that some couldn’t make it because of the sudden flight ground-stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration around 12:30 p.m. PT. Whether human or AI, aviation afflictions come for us all.
	

	The guests gracing the red carpet were not screens rolled out displaying AI avatars, contrary to a reasonable assumption. Instead, the human creators behind the digital faces strutted the carpet in their Sunday best, treating the night less as music’s biggest night and more as the biggest night for their music. Sequined dresses and colorful blazers strolled through, stopping to speak with outlets like Reuters to the fiery red mohawk-sporting, sequin-wearing host of “The Iconic Punk Oz” Oz Powers to, tucked against a wall and steps from the red carpet, an effective AI red carpet correspondent housed inside a tall, white faux-stone vessel. The contraption was developed by the event’s top sponsor, Deepgram, an AI startup specializing in text-to-speech agents.

	The device, which knew the artists and pressed them about the event, struck in me a slight fear about whether people might opt for robot reporters instead of humans, though that fear subsided when I realized this device could not appear on the red carpet because it could not move. The creators seemed more eager to speak to the physical reporters anyway, with some of them emphasizing the human elements of their AI work. Fredro Starr, one half of the rap group Onyx, spent much of the carpet touting the human vocals that made up his AI-beat-laden record “It All Started in Brooklyn,” which he claimed was the first AI album on vinyl.

	“You can’t replace [humans],” Starr told me, using the carpet to debut his new moniker, “Mad AI.” “The feeling that you get was what we bring with the spirit of hip-hop. So vocally, you can hear that, but the AI just took it to another level.”

	Inside the theater, SIQA tried to bring a party-like feel to the function. A bar at the back of the venue —at a charge — kept well drinks flowing, and the bar top was littered with copies of a sponsored version of the newspaper “Rolling Out” featuring interviews with many of the nominees and James, the SIQA founder. One of those featured, Xania Monet founder Jones, sparked a wave of controversy last year when some of her Monet songs hit some of Billboard’s genre charts, leading to an interview with CBS’s Gayle King and to Kehlani slamming a $3 million record deal Jones received. As she waited for a drink by the bar ahead of the event’s start, Jones told me she wasn’t worried about the AI of it all overshadowing the pursuit of legitimacy within the greater music industry.
	

	“AI is just a tool,” she said. “It just emphasizes what we do. I just feel like we should all be one.”

	But despite that lofty goal, the kinks kept rearing their heads.

	The event started about 30 minutes past its 6:15 p.m. start time, skipping a planned opening video montage for a dance break performed and choreographed by actor Giovanni Wilson with eight dancers to a seemingly AI-produced song that described — in literal terms — how we were at the inaugural AI music awards. The delay forced the show to skip introducing the nominees for the first half of the awards and instead have presenters just state the winner, robbing some attendees of hearing their names called for what felt like one of their biggest achievements.

	The event was hosted by Wilson and podcast host Lana Hout, one half of the podcasting duo the “AI Chicks,” with a three-member house band of real people playing guitar, bass, keys and drums, soundtracking much of the night. The two hosts shared the only two microphones apparently available throughout the night, with a teleprompter loaded with the Claude-generated run-of-show, but they often seemed lost about what category, presenter, performance or commercial break was next.

	At one point, Hout and Wilson were confused over whether they would cut to commercial or bring out the two presenters for best AI country artist. They then brought out the two country award presenters, only for Hout to walk back out mid-introduction to interrupt and say that, actually, they would go to commercial break. The award was eventually presented 13 minutes later with a different presenter.

	Oftentimes, the use of AI seemed to hover over some of the technical hiccups. Deepgram was meant to power an AI voice that introduced the night’s presenters and nominees, but it often didn’t work and, when it did, talked over many of the presenters. Deepgram also had a commercial that played throughout the evening, but it would sometimes play at random moments even when a commercial break wasn’t called. The Deepgram team sat on the couch to my left, and when I looked over to see their reaction to the madness, one member had her head in her hands.

	Early in the night, Wilson tried to introduce a trailer for his latest acting gig, the Terrance Howard-led film “A Good Hand Wasted” that he said used AI to help finish the project, but none of Wilson’s cues seemed to get it to play. Once it finally did, the screen only played a portion of the trailer before Howard’s face even appeared.
	

	“So, ugh,” he said, before raising his hand to summon the audience’s applause.

	The teleprompter was not much help, often shifting rapidly as presenters were speaking. The chaos led Wilson, who spent much of the night trying to maintain some decorum throughout the frustration, to joke they were “dealing with a prompter that has Tourette’s.”

	The commercials for the event featured Deepgram and a new social network called “Trinity Social,” with the latter’s AI-generated ad featuring a persona wearing a necklace of the Rockstar Games logo encouraging a stadium full of generated people to sign up for the app. A Rockstar spokesperson did not respond to an immediate request for comment on whether it authorized the logo, though if it did not, the ad would represent the latest in AI content lifting copyrighted material without permission, all at an event celebrating a use of AI that has rankled the music industry over similar concerns.

	Some of the greatest energy came from the evening’s nearly 10 performances, all of which made the cut despite the event running nearly 40 minutes behind schedule the entire night. 

	There had been some speculation over how, exactly, songs produced with AI and presented by AI avatars would play on stage. It turns out, through the power of lip-syncing and acting. Some acts, like country artist Ava Bentley and R&B artist EJ Rogers, lip-synced their entire performance, while others relied on hired performers who did even that for them. For “Chaisen Hale,” a project that features a video of an AI-generated boy with AI-generated vocals, a human lookalike singer named John Victor, 14, was brought out to lip-sync to the track. Attendees — including one duo, for some reason, dressed as Frankenstein and his bride — were generally riveted.

	Nearly all of the performances were backed by the live band and dancers, who were provided to the artists for free by SIQA. Many who produce music with AI say they did so because they could not afford the studio musicians and resources required to bring their tracks to life, which made the reliance on the house band feel more like an opportunity to live out their dreams without the cost often paid by traditional artists who hire such musicians to produce their work.
	

	Some of the only actual live vocals came from a rapper named GodFellow and Grammy-winning singers Eric Bellinger and Candace Wakefield, the latter of whom made a point to note the “hiccups” throughout the night and that she was singing live as she performed a song by AI artist “Aria Blue.” The performances captured much of what remained in the crowd, which grew smaller and smaller as the night progressed.

	James, the SIQA founder, acknowledged the “technical difficulties” ahead of presenting Jones with her awards, but she promised those would be resolved ahead of next year’s ceremony.

	“Because there will be a next year because this is the new music industry,” she told the crowd around 9:45 p.m., just as it was hitting its hard end time. ”SIQA has created the infrastructure for that industry and for all the artists coming up in that industry.”

	And for many of the people in the room, that’s all they wanted. One artist, Sheena Taylor, accepted her award for best AI gospel song for a track called “I Denounce You, Satan,” by acknowledging the intense traumas she endured that led to a religious discovery. Another artist named Ramona Höffel, a 56-year-old woman who spends her days helping disabled people, flew in from Switzerland to represent her AI persona “Vireya” on her first-ever red carpet. (When I addressed her by her given name, she snapped at me.)

	“I have a lot of ideas and wishes, and for a long time I paint, then I write, and that’s not enough,” she said, visibly nervous to be the first person to walk the red carpet. “The music gives me room to all this bring outside of my brain.”

	I thought about Höffel’s words as I left the venue just after 10 p.m., well past the event’s scheduled 9:30 end, and into the downtown rain. To my right was a line forming to get into the venue for “Club 2010s” night, now delayed due to the prolonged awards show. It’s unclear whether AI music will generate an enduring monoculture in the way the music from the 2010s has, particularly as the larger music industry has mostly ostracized it. But it’s left people like Höffel feeling stronger, which is all someone like 2011 chart-topper Kelly Clarkson could ask for.

schema.headline: Inside the First AI Music Awards, a Chaotic Evening Attempting to Normalize Tech-Assisted Tunes

title: Is ‘Club Kid’ a ‘Conservative’ Movie? Only If You’re Still Living in the ’60s
description: One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as s
body:
One of the things I love about movies is how layered they are. When a film connects on a deep level, saying what it’s truly “about” may not be as simple as it sounds. Chasing down a movie’s inner meaning can lead you into the mystery of things. A great movie can be “about” more than it seems.

	Take “Club Kid.” Jordan Firstman’s ebullient and moving first feature tells a story that couldn’t be more straightforward — or, in a way, more traditional. Firstman, who gives a fantastic performance, plays Peter, a queer New York party promoter (a few decades ago we would have called him “downtown,” now he’s Brooklyn) who learns that he has a 9-year-old son, whom he fathered in a random three-way sexual encounter at one of his 4:00 a.m. club bacchanals. The kid, Arlo (Reggie Absolom), is sweet and curly-haired and British (he arrives with a chaperone from London); his mother, who raised him, recently committed suicide. The responsibility to take care of Arlo has suddenly dropped on Peter like a load of bricks. It’s something he doesn’t want and, for the time being, doesn’t have much choice about. But as he and the kid start to hang out, a tentative relationship forms, and the two begin to figure out what they might mean to each other.
	

	What “Club Kid” is “about” is how Peter, a charming dissolute man-child, living an existence of unhinged hedonism, discovers that he wants to grow up and take care of someone besides himself. On that score, the drama is authentic and fully felt. In outline, though, it’s something we’ve seen many times before, in films from “About a Boy” to “Big Daddy.” Yet what makes “Club Kid” singular is that it’s about something larger than that.
	

	As a filmmaker, Firstman plunges you into the world of queer club culture with a fervor and tumult and personality and lived-in detail that takes your breath away. He plunks the audience down in the middle of the shade-throwing nightbloom revels, the cocaine and ketamine binges, so that we experience the cathartic rush of drugged-out insolence, of heightened erotic excitement, of gender-flipping transgression. From the earliest days of gay liberation, the party scene was a core expression of queer freedom, and still is. What we call disco started in the underground gay clubs of the early ’70s, and part of Peter’s cachet as a promoter is that what’s he organizing is now a business, but it’s still underground. The staging of these scenes, and the acting in them, is extraordinary. Jordan Firstman makes us feel the life of the party.

	And yet…he’s not merely celebrating it. Far from it. As authentic and scene-specific as they are, the party sequences in “Club Kid” signify as more than just a portrayal of the New York queer club scene. They’re also a larger snapshot of what party culture, out there in the world, has become: an arena of liberation that’s rooted in a place of physical and spiritual abandon that contains the seeds of destruction.

	If you wanted to encapsulate the history of the last six decades in one sentence, you could do worse than this: Ever since the late ’60s, the party has never stopped. There are countless versions of the party, and we’ve all been to our own preferred versions. It might have been the singles bars of the disco age, or the frat-house benders that came to rule in the late ’70s — and have only grown more frenzied and predatory ever since. It might have been the industrial dance clubs of the ’80s or the raves of the ’90s. It might have been the suburban saturnalia of “Jersey Shore,” or the more contempo versions of that. It might have been the punk mosh pits, or the revels of Studio 54, or the back-to-the-underground scene of Basement. The music, the drugs, the alcohol, the hooking up, the vibe of orgiastic excess — for 60 years now, we’ve been a culture on the prowl.

	In “Club Kid,” it’s not just Peter who starts to question the party culture that has fueled him. The film itself is questioning it. It’s asking, “Is this how we should be living?” And yet, because the movie dares to pose that question, there has been a backlash against it, with a chorus of voices damning the movie by branding it “conservative.” A certain number of people are looking at “Club Kid,” with its tale of a queer man who turns his back on his own personal decadence to embrace the call of family, as if it were a movie Nancy Reagan could love.
	

	What I think the “conservative” slur misses is that Jordan Firstman, who came out of this scene, is not questioning it in a puritanical or moralistic way. He captures the honest vibrance of party culture. Yet he also captures — and this is what I think is brilliant about “Club Kid” — that whatever version of it floats your boat, the party that never stops, while rooted in a certain vibe of community, may be rooted even more deeply in the enticement we feel from getting high on ourselves. That’s the hidden seduction of party culture, the thrill and the beauty of it, and maybe the lie of it. The party doesn’t need to stop. But it might be time that we stopped seeing it as an uncut salvation without ever pausing to ask, as “Club Kid” does, what it’s doing to us.

schema.headline: Is ‘Club Kid’ a ‘Conservative’ Movie? Only If You’re Still Living in the ’60s

body:
Inside the Camgirl Criminal Empire
                          Women Tricked Into Working for Almost Nothing
                      
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            Nikita Tyukalo allegedly lured young women into his camgirl empire with promises of fame and fortune ... only to take control of their accounts and leave them with little to none of the cash they were bringing in.
      
    
            Our new documentary, "TMZ Studios Presents: Inside the Camgirl Criminal Empire," is now streaming on YouTube ... exposing how Nikita allegedly built a fortune through manipulation, coercion, and exploitation.
      
    
            According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Nikita allegedly recruited women by promising big paydays and exposure ... even telling one girlfriend that creating explicit content could help cover her school bills.
      

            But once the women signed on, Nikita allegedly changed their OnlyFans login information ... locking them out of their account and leaving them in the dark about how much money they were making.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            And the alleged scheme didn't stop there ... an investigator claims that Nikita used "bot-boosting" to artificially inflate viewership and push his camgirls higher on streaming platforms, all while flaunting luxury cars, properties and lavish parties.
      
    
            Meanwhile, the women were allegedly streaming nearly around the clock for little to no pay ... until a band of camgirl superfans began digging into the operation and helped bring it crashing down.
      
    
            "TMZ Studios Presents: Inside the Camgirl Criminal Empire" is now streaming on YouTube.

title: High School Football Player Dies After Being Declared Brain Dead Following Collapse

body:
H.S. School Football Player
                          Dies After Being Declared Brain Dead, Gym Collapse
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A high school student who collapsed in the middle of gym class has died after the medical emergency left him brain dead.
      
    
            Levi Curry -- who was a rising defensive star on the Eagle River High School football team in Anchorage, Alaska -- went into cardiac arrest during the gym class on Nov. 6 ... according to his GoFundMe.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Later that night, Levi was declared brain dead.
      

            Apparently, Levi suffered from a pre-existing heart condition that was managed by a pediatric cardiologist ... his church shared.
      
    
            Levi's dad James told KTUU that his son had undergone surgery that "basically healed it."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After his parents made the tough decision to proceed with organ donation, Levi died on Nov. 7.
      
    
            Nearly 500 people showed up to pay their respects at Levi's funeral ... PEOPLE reported.
      
    
            He was only 15 years old.

title: Port of New Orleans Sues Tanker & Its Owners After Cruise Ship Crash
description:
Riverboat Collision
                          Port of New Orleans Sues Freighter Over Cruise Ship
body:
Riverboat Collision
                          Port of New Orleans Sues Freighter Over Cruise Ship Crash
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The Port of New Orleans has sued the owners of the tanker that crashed into a cruise ship ... claiming more than $1 million in potential damage.
      
    
            In addition to the owners, the tanker's management and the ship itself are also listed as defendants in their federal suit ... 4WWL reported.
      
    
        
                    
                  
      
    
            The port also said it doesn't know the full extent of the damages and repairs needed for the port terminal and asked a judge to approve the seizure of the tanker -- Atlantic Asphalt -- so it could potentially be sold to help pay for the repairs.
      

            The bottom line ... the port believes the tanker and its companies failed to follow safety regulations and act in time to avoid colliding with the river cruise ship, American Heritage.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            On Friday night, a federal warrant was issued authorizing the tanker's seizure.
      
    
            As a result of the collision and the cruise ship capsizing, 32 people were injured and taken to local hospitals.
